cards.front: What kind of service is Amazon CloudFront, and what is its main benefit?
cards.back: A global **content delivery network (CDN)**. It caches copies of your content at edge locations close to viewers, which cuts latency and takes load off the origin.

cards.front: On a CloudFront cache miss, where does the edge location look next?
cards.back: Usually the nearest **regional edge cache** (a larger, mid-tier cache). Only if that also misses does CloudFront fetch from the **origin**, then it stores the object in both caches. Dynamic requests and PUT/POST/DELETE skip the regional cache.

cards.front: Name the four kinds of CloudFront origins covered in this lesson.
cards.back: 1) **S3 bucket** (REST endpoint, secured with OAC), 2) **S3 static website endpoint** (as a custom origin), 3) **custom HTTP origin** such as a public ALB or EC2 instance, 4) **VPC origin** for a private ALB, NLB or EC2 instance.

cards.front: How do you make a private S3 bucket readable only through CloudFront?
cards.back: Attach an **Origin Access Control (OAC)** to the S3 origin and add a **bucket policy** that allows the principal `cloudfront.amazonaws.com` (for example `s3:GetObject`) with the condition `AWS:SourceArn` = the distribution ARN. Keep Block Public Access on.

cards.front: Why choose OAC over the older OAI?
cards.back: OAC works with buckets in **all Regions** (including opt-in ones), supports **SSE-KMS** encrypted objects and supports **PUT/DELETE**, so uploads through CloudFront work. OAI is legacy and lacks these.

cards.front: Can you use OAC with an S3 static website endpoint origin?
cards.back: **No.** A website endpoint is treated as a custom HTTP origin, so OAC/OAI cannot be used; the objects must be public and CloudFront talks to it over HTTP only.

cards.front: An internet-facing ALB is a CloudFront origin. How do you stop people bypassing CloudFront?
cards.back: Allow only the **CloudFront managed prefix list** (`com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing`) in the ALB security group, and have CloudFront add a **secret custom header** that an ALB listener rule requires (default rule returns 403). Use HTTPS to the origin.
cards.updated: Slides point to a published IP list; the managed prefix list is the current method.

cards.front: What does a CloudFront VPC origin let you do?
cards.back: Serve an **internal ALB, internal NLB or EC2 instance in a private subnet** through CloudFront with no public IP or internet-facing load balancer. CloudFront uses a service-managed ENI in the subnet; the VPC still needs an internet gateway attached.
cards.updated: Current docs add limits: no GWLB, no NLB TLS listeners, NLB needs a security group.

cards.front: With a plain custom origin (not a VPC origin), must the ALB in front of your EC2 instances be public?
cards.back: **Yes**, the ALB must be internet-facing because CloudFront reaches custom origins over the internet. The EC2 instances behind it can stay private and allow only the ALB's security group.

cards.front: What is CloudFront's default TTL when the origin sends no caching headers (CachingOptimized policy)?
cards.back: **24 hours** (86,400 seconds). That policy's minimum is 1 second and its maximum 365 days (31,536,000 seconds).

cards.front: You updated a file in the S3 origin but viewers still get the old copy. What are your two options?
cards.back: Create a **CloudFront invalidation** for the path (for example `/index.html` or `/images/*`), or use **versioned file names** so the new file has a new URL. AWS recommends versioning for files that change often.

cards.front: How are CloudFront invalidations priced?
cards.back: The first **1,000 paths per month** per account are free, then **USD 0.005 per path**. A wildcard path such as `/images/*` counts as **one** path no matter how many files it clears.

cards.front: Where can the `*` wildcard appear in a CloudFront invalidation path?
cards.back: Only as the **last character**, for example `/images/*` or `/*`. Paths are case sensitive.

cards.front: What are the two modes of CloudFront geo restriction, and what does a blocked viewer receive?
cards.back: An **allow list** (only listed countries are served) or a **block list** (listed countries are refused). Blocked viewers get **HTTP 403 Forbidden**, optionally with a custom error page.

cards.front: What are the main limits of CloudFront's built-in geo restriction?
cards.back: It works only at **country level** (via a third-party GeoIP database, about 99.8% accurate) and applies to the **entire distribution**. Per-path or city-level rules need WAF geo match rules, separate distributions or a third-party service.

cards.front: CloudFront or S3 Cross-Region Replication: which fits frequently updated objects needed with low latency in two specific Regions?
cards.back: **S3 Cross-Region Replication.** It keeps near-real-time copies in the Regions you choose. CloudFront fits content needed everywhere that can tolerate TTL-based caching.

cards.front: Unicast versus anycast IP: what is the difference?
cards.back: **Unicast**: one IP belongs to one server. **Anycast**: many servers in different places announce the same IP, and routing delivers each client to the nearest one.

cards.front: How many static IP addresses does a Global Accelerator standard accelerator provide?
cards.back: **Two static anycast IPv4 addresses** (from Amazon's pool or your own BYOIP range). A **dual-stack** accelerator gets four: two IPv4 and two IPv6.
cards.updated: Dual-stack (2 IPv4 + 2 IPv6) is newer than the slides' two-IP description.

cards.front: Which endpoint types can a Global Accelerator standard accelerator route to?
cards.back: **Application Load Balancers, Network Load Balancers** (each internet-facing or internal), **EC2 instances** and **Elastic IP addresses**, in one or more Regions.

cards.front: Why does Global Accelerator avoid the DNS caching problem of DNS-based failover?
cards.back: Clients always connect to the **same static IPs**. When an endpoint fails a health check, the edge sends new connections to another healthy endpoint or Region; no DNS record changes, so cached DNS answers do not matter.

cards.front: Global Accelerator: what is a traffic dial versus an endpoint weight?
cards.back: A **traffic dial** (0–100%, per endpoint group/Region) limits how much of the traffic headed to that Region it accepts. A **weight** (0–255, default 128, per endpoint) splits traffic among endpoints inside a group.

cards.front: What health check settings can you tune for Global Accelerator EC2 or Elastic IP endpoints?
cards.back: Protocol (TCP by default, or HTTP/HTTPS with a path), port, interval of **10 or 30 seconds** (default 30) and threshold count (default **3**). ALB/NLB endpoints use the load balancer's own target health checks.

cards.front: Does Global Accelerator cache content at the edge?
cards.back: **No.** It only proxies TCP/UDP connections over the AWS backbone to your endpoints. Caching at the edge is CloudFront's job.

cards.front: Give three workloads that point to Global Accelerator rather than CloudFront.
cards.back: Non-HTTP traffic such as **online gaming over UDP**, **IoT over MQTT** or **VoIP**; HTTP apps that need **static IPs** to allow-list; apps needing **deterministic, fast regional failover**.

cards.front: Which DDoS and firewall protections come with CloudFront and Global Accelerator?
cards.back: Both get **AWS Shield Standard** automatically at no extra cost (Shield Advanced is optional). CloudFront can also attach an **AWS WAF** web ACL to filter HTTP requests at the edge.

cards.front: How is AWS Global Accelerator billed?
cards.back: **USD 0.025 per accelerator-hour** (partial hours count as full, enabled or disabled) plus a per-GB **DT-Premium** fee, plus **USD 0.005 per hour** for each static public IPv4 address. No free tier.

cards.front: In which Region must an ACM certificate live to serve HTTPS for a CloudFront alternate domain name?
cards.back: **us-east-1 (N. Virginia)**, regardless of where the origin runs. A certificate for an ALB origin stays in the ALB's own Region.

cards.front: What does CloudFront's Always Free tier include each month?
cards.back: **1 TB** of data transfer out, **10 million** HTTP/HTTPS requests and **2 million** CloudFront Functions invocations (plus 2 million KeyValueStore reads).

cards.front: How can you lower CloudFront delivery cost by limiting which edge locations serve your content?
cards.back: Pick a cheaper **price class**. **Price Class 100** uses only North America and Europe (plus Israel and Türkiye); **Price Class 200** leaves out only South America and Australia/New Zealand. Viewers outside the class are still served, from a farther edge.
